To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

monensin supplementation improves performance of broiler chicks infected with Eimeria acerulina and that the adverse effects of feeding a high level (140 mg/kg diet) of monensin can be mitigated by increasing dietary crude protein to 28%.

1) the adverse effects of high dietary monensin on performance are more pronounced when the dietary protein level is low; 2) the adverse effect of high dietary monensen on performance in chicks fed low dietary protein diets is largely due to its anorectic properties; and 3) the growth depression induced by high dietary monensn is greater in Eimeria acerulina infected than uninfected chicks.
monensin supplementation improved performance of broiler chicks fed 16 or 20% CP, but not 24% CP diets.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the influence of dietary protein level on the growth response to ionophore supplementation in broilers.
the influence of several factors on the response of broiler chicks to dietary monensin.
the interrelationship between dietary protein and monen-sin.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the adverse effects of high levels of monensin in low protein diets were due primarily to the anorexic properties of monensin.

monensin supplementation of corn-soybean broiler diets containing 16% protein results in a greater reduction in weight gain than when the diets contain 24% protein, and that the adverse effects of feeding monensin to low protein diets can be attributed to the anorexic properties of monensin.

monensin supplementation of broiler diets containing 16% CP is detrimental to performance, and that the adverse effects of feeding low protein diets to broiler chicks can be alleviated to a considerable extent by increasing dietary protein level or by feeding a higher protein diet to pair-fed chicks.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the growth response to monensin supplementation was greater in chicks fed diets containing low protein and that this response could be partially attributed to the anorexic properties of monensin.
the monensin growth depression observed in low protein diets is largely due to the anorexic effects of monens in combination with the reduced ability of low protein diets to sustain growth.
monensin supplementation of low CP diets is detrimental, whereas high CP diets are less susceptible to monensin's growth-depressant effects.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the growth depression induced by feeding high levels of monensin can be moderated by feeding high levels (28% CP) of protein.
the monensin level and protein level interaction is not as pronounced as previously reported.
the adverse effects of feeding high levels of monensin to chicks fed low protein, corn-soybean-meal-based diets are due to its anorexia properties.
